Introduction
Adult spine deformity (ASD)
Abnormal alignment of the spinal column in a skeletally mature individual
Comprises a wide spectrum of diseases and diagnoses
Deformities may occur in the coronal, sagittal, and axial planes.
Cause loss of local, regional, and/or global alignment
May result in an imbalance of the spinal column
An inability to stand in the cone of economy and maintain upright posture with minimal
energy expenditure
Center of mass of the head normally lies over the weight-bearing axis of the body.
Instability is the inability of the spine to maintain physiologic loads without neural
compromise, deformity, or intractable pain.
Sagittal balance
The cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine regions have balanced and proportional sagittal
curvatures to maintain upright posture and efficient ambulation.
Primary (thoracic, sacral) alignments and acquired (cervical, lumbar) alignments, the latter
of which develops with crawling then upright posture and walking
Reciprocal to pelvic alignment
Sagittal alignment may be balanced, compensated, or imbalanced.
Increasing energy expenditure to maintain balance results in increased deformity, pain,
and disability.
Sagittal imbalance is associated with disability and lower health-related quality of life
(HRQOL) scores.
General descriptions of the deformity include
Coronal: scoliosis
Sagittal: kyphosis (anterior curvature) or lordosis (posterior curvature)
Axial: olisthesis (subluxation) with rotation or translation

Introduction
ASD describes an abnormal alignment of the spinal column in a skeletally mature
individual1 and includes a wide spectrum of pathologic spine deformities. Deformities
may occur in any plane and lead to local, regional, or global malalignment (Resource 1).

ASD may result in an imbalance of the spinal column, defined as a loss of stable upright
posture under normal physiologic load. Global coronal and sagittal balance are
described by the vertical relationship of the center of mass of the head over that of the
body, pelvis, and center of rotation of the femoral heads. Typically, scoliosis is defined by
a coronal deformity with a Cobb angle greater than 10°; however, sagittal deformities
are common and may lead to substantial disability.
The mobile cervical, thoracic, and lumbar regions of the spine have characteristic
curvatures in the sagittal plane2 (Figure 1).

Balance of the sagittal curvatures and proportionate spinopelvic alignment are required
to maintain vertical body posture with minimal energy expenditure and horizontal gaze
for ambulation. Dubousset introduced the concept of a cone of economy, defined as a
zone of postures in which balance is maintained with limited effort and motion can be
readily accommodated3 (Figure 2; Resource 2).
Figure 2 Illustration of the human skeleton shows the Dubousset cone of economy.
Normally, if humans assume an erect posture, they stand within a certain zone of
balance in which the torso remains within a certain distance from the pelvis. By doing
this, energy expended by the postural muscles is minimized. Beyond this zone, the cone
of economy, energy expenditure rapidly increases, and eventually spinal misalignment
results. (Reproduced with permission from Kenneth Xavier Probst/Xavier Studio, San
Rafael, CA, 2012.)

Sagittal imbalance is associated with loss of efficient energy expenditure as spinal
alignment falls outside the cone of economy. Any deformity may be balanced, balanced
with compensation, or imbalanced. Compensatory changes that maintain global balance
typically include thoracic lordosis, pelvic retroversion, hip and knee flexion, and ankle
dorsiflexion4,5 (Figure 3). These expected changes are required to maintain balance but
will increase energy expenditure. Failure of compensation may occur with progression of
deformity, inadequate conditioning, and contractures that prevent compensation.
Sagittal balance is then lost, leading to pain, degeneration, additional deformity, and
progressive disability as measured by HRQOL scores (Video 1).


Epidemiology
ASD is increasingly prevalent with the aging population. Prevalence ranges from 8.3% to
68% and is approximately equal between women and men.6 Prevalence and severity
increase with age, with more than on-half of patients 60 years or older having a
deformity observed on radiographs. Given the broad spectrum of disease severity, the
most common deformities are mild. Sagittal imbalance has been reported in 14% to
30.4% of individuals.7 As the prevalence rises, the rate of surgical management
increases.
Anatomy and Etiology
In general, cervical (C1 through C7) and lumbar (L1 through L5) segments are lordotic, and
thoracic (T1 through T12) segments are kyphotic.
The thoracic spine is constrained by the ribs and sternum.
The Roussouly classification system has proposed four sagittal plane alignments in which
sacral slope guides lordotic and kyphotic segments.8
The relationship of the spine to the pelvis and the hip center of rotation is defined as
spinopelvic alignment.
Spinal alignment must be proportional to pelvic alignment to achieve upright posture.
Scoliosis in ASD commonly results from primary degeneration (type 1; de novo) or progression
of adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (type 2) or occurs secondary to another pathology (type 3).
Iatrogenic, metabolic bone disease, fracture, inflammatory disorders, neuromuscular
disorders, pelvic deformity, leg-length discrepancies, pathologic, congenital, and other
degenerative etiologies
Various etiologies may contribute to sagittal imbalance.
Sagittal imbalance occurs if vertical posture cannot be maintained under physiologic loads.
Typically from an abnormal deficiency of lordosis or exaggeration of kyphosis
Loss of anterior column height or failure of the posterior tension band may result in kyphosis
and sagittal imbalance.
Common etiologies are similar to those of coronal deformities: degeneration, trauma,
osteoporosis, iatrogenic, inflammatory, sarcopenia, neuromuscular, congenital, infectious,
pathologic, etc.

Compensatory mechanisms are normal responses to sagittal deformity to maintain
alignment.
Loss of joint motion (eg, hip flexion contracture or osteoarthritis) or muscle atrophy (eg,
paraspinal, psoas, or hip extensor) results in failure of compensation.
Sagittal imbalance may result from forward flexion to limit pain from stenosis and must be
differentiated from structural deformity.

Anatomy and Etiology
Sagittal balance requires harmonious cervical, thoracic, and lumbar curvatures, in which
alignment is driven by pelvic parameters, such as the pelvic incidence. Spinopelvic
alignment, defined by the relationship of the spine to the pelvis and, consequently, the
hip center of rotation, influences the magnitude of sagittal curvature required to
maintain upright posture with minimal energy expenditure. Thoracic motion is
constrained by the ribs and sternum. Transitional segments and congenital or
developmental structural abnormalities also can affect regional spinal alignment. In ASD,
scoliosis may result from primary degeneration or progression of adolescent idiopathic
scoliosis or occur secondary to other etiologies (Table 1). Sagittal imbalance also may
result from these etiologies if they affect sagittal alignment.

Sarcopenia with paraspinal or hip extensor atrophy and neuromuscular disorders limit

resulting in fatigue and disability. In particular, Parkinsonian disorders lead to early,

muscular strength and joint motion. Compensatory mechanisms engaged include pelvic
retroversion (increasing pelvic tilt), hip and knee flexion, thoracic and cervical

extensors, results in failure of compensation and worsening sagittal imbalance. Pain
from stenosis also may result in a functional sagittal imbalance without structural
deformity and must be recognized9 (Video 2).

Patient History
Assessment of ASD requires a thorough patient history and physical examination. Onset
and progression of symptoms; characterization of pain; assessment of disability;
previous management; and a complete medical, surgical, and social history are essential.
Patients may have a known history of idiopathic scoliosis, previous surgical treatment, or
other pathology. Care must be taken to identify associated comorbidities affecting the
deformity or potential surgical management, including osteoporosis, nicotine use,
malnutrition, and primary muscular atrophy. Diagnosis of neuromuscular disorders,
such as Parkinson disease, is imperative given the notorious rate of surgical failure in
these patients. Patients with a radiographic deformity may be asymptomatic, or
symptoms may be associated with other degenerative or musculoskeletal pathology,
requiring a detailed and focused evaluation.
The presentation of sagittal imbalance may vary considerably based on etiology,
associated degenerative disorders, and the extent of regional and global compensation.
Patients most commonly present with back pain, particularly with standing and activity.
Back pain will worsen with progressive imbalance and become associated with greater

Physical Examination
A focused but complete physical examination supplements the patient history. The
patient should be appropriately disrobed to allow for complete evaluation of the
deformity. The physical examination should be performed in the standing and supine
positions or the prone position to assess changes in alignment and curve rigidity.
Standing coronal and sagittal balance (truncal shift; Figure 6) and global, regional, and
local alignment must be assessed. Shoulder and pelvic obliquities, rib prominence, and
leg-length discrepancies should be identified.

Radiography
Radiographs are indicated in the initial evaluation of a spinal deformity or deformity
progression and should be obtained if a local, regional, or global deformity is suspected.
PA and lateral long radiographs (36-inch) are necessary to visualize the entire spine and

Nonsurgical treatment may be considered in patients with ASD and sagittal imbalance

Nonsurgical treatment options include physical therapy and exercise, medications,

Surgical Techniques
Reduction of sagittal deformity is a challenge. Mobile segments are required, often
necessitating releases or osteotomies, rigid fixation, and various realignment
techniques. The flexibility of a deformity must be evaluated during the physical
examination and with radiographs to plan adequately. Specific techniques are then
selected based on the degree and type of deformity. Mild, flexible deformities with
multiple open segments can be corrected via instrumentation and positioning alone.

or rigid deformities require additional releases or osteotomies to allow for realignment.
Open disk spaces allow for anterior release, including anterior column releases that

correction per level. In the thoracic spine, releases are limited by the sternum and ribs.

Complications
Surgical complications are common in the management of ASD and sagittal imbalance,
with rates frequently exceeding 55%.31 Complication rates in the management of fixed
sagittal imbalance also are high (as high as 29.4%).32 Complications range from minor
(eg, urinary tract infection, superficial wound infection, postoperative ileus, transient
neuropraxia) to major (eg, neurologic deficit, pulmonary embolism, major cardiac event,
death). Most complications occur in the acute postoperative period, peaking within 3
months postoperatively; however, some occur bimodally, with PJK/PJF and implant
failure peaking after 24 months postoperatively.33 Common complications (69.8% at 2
years postoperatively) by category include implant-related (27.8%), radiographic (27.8%),
neurologic (27.8%), surgical (25.4%), cardiopulmonary (18.9%), infection (14.8%), and

Common Complications
ASD is associated with several common complications that require heightened
awareness for prevention and management. Implant-related complications, including
rod fracture and instrumentation failure, are common. They are more frequent with
pseudarthrosis and may occur at junctional levels or at the site of three-column

reduces pseudarthrosis and instrumentation failure at the lumbosacral junction. In
addition, PJK is common, occurring in 10% to 40% of patients; however, PJF requiring
revision surgery is much less common, ranging from 1% to 5%38 (Figure 15). Avoidance
of PJK is a challenge38 (Table 12).

Surgical management of ASD with sagittal imbalance may result in improvement in pain,
function, and HRQOL measures. Multiple studies have shown improvement in back pain,
leg pain, and function that is inverse to the magnitude of deformity. Older patients
experience clinical improvement and need not be excluded if they are well-optimized

depression, increased body mass index, comorbidities, disability, residual deformity

Several sagittal alignment parameters have been associated with pain, disability, and
HRQOL measures preoperatively and postoperatively.23 Limited evidence exists for age-
appropriate alignment goals and proportional restoration of sagittal balance in
improving postoperative outcomes and reducing mechanical complications;14,24

restoration of sagittal alignment versus nonsurgical management has remained limited,
with only low-quality evidence available for parameters such as pelvic tilt.12 The authors
of a recent meta-analysis were unable to complete the analysis for many of the existing
studies because of incomplete reporting of data.
